system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-12-19 18:17:00 to 2156-12-21 16:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, following a recent hospitalization for similar symptoms. She has a complex history including chronic graft-versus-host disease, gastroparesis, and immunosuppression. Initial evaluation revealed metabolic acidosis and leukocytosis. Imaging showed no acute abdominal pathology but mild colitis on MRI. Stool testing confirmed rotavirus infection, explaining her gastroenteritis. She also had a complicated UTI with Enterococcus, treated with nitrofurantoin. During her stay, she received IV fluids, antiemetics, and supportive care, with gradual improvement. She tolerated oral intake, and symptoms resolved. A sacral bone marrow finding on MRI prompted a recommendation for outpatient pelvic MRI to rule out infiltrative disease. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans, including completing antibiotics, restarting bowel regimen when appropriate, and coordinating outpatient imaging and IVIG.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Chronic venous embolism and thrombosis of unspecified deep vessels of lower extremity

diagnoses.long_title: Closed fracture of seventh cervical vertebra
Complications of transplanted organ, stem cell
Closed fracture of dorsal [thoracic] vertebra without mention of spinal cord injury
Other restorative surgery causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you had a scary event today—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I was sitting in the waiting room for my cognitive neurology appointment. I started feeling really lightheaded, like the room was spinning. Then I think I passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you hit your head or feel any pain when you lost consciousness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, my husband said I just slumped over. He called for help, and someone started doing chest compressions. I don’t remember that part, but I woke up quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That must have been frightening. Your blood pressure was very low when EMS arrived—around 56 over 35. Did you eat or drink anything this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I skipped breakfast. I wasn’t hungry and wanted to get to the appointment on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We’re going to give you IV fluids to help stabilize your blood pressure. We also did an EKG, and it showed some changes, so cardiology came to see you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology reviewed your EKG and blood tests. Your troponin levels—those check for heart damage—were normal. They don’t think you had a heart attack. The EKG changes might be related to the low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The most likely cause is low blood volume—what we call hypovolemia. Skipping meals and fluids, especially with your medical history, can make you more prone to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel dizzy sometimes, even when I’m not fasting. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll monitor you closely. You’re on a heart monitor now to check for any rhythm issues. We also ordered a CT scan of your chest to rule out a blood clot in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had blood clots before, so I’m glad we’re checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no pulmonary embolism or aortic issues. But it did show some mild compression in your spine, at C7 and T2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My spine? I didn’t fall or feel any pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The neurosurgeon looked at it and said these are likely old fractures, possibly from your past osteoporosis or transplant-related bone changes. Since you’re not having neck or back pain, they don’t need treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several compression fractures before—T11, L1. So this might be similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that fits. We’ll make sure your bone health is followed up with your oncologist. For now, we’re focusing on keeping your blood pressure stable with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some juice and toast this morning and haven’t felt dizzy at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood pressure is now 118 over 70, and your repeat labs show improvement in your acid levels and lactate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What was wrong with my acid levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When your blood pressure dropped, your body wasn’t getting enough oxygen, which caused a mild metabolic acidosis. That’s improving now with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my heart monitor—any issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No arrhythmias. Cardiology noted a slightly prolonged QT interval on your EKG, which is something we watch with some of your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis. Could that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Fluconazole can prolong the QT interval. After talking with your transplant team, we’ve decided to stop it for now. You should follow up with them about whether to restart it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call them. I just don’t want to get an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on acyclovir and Bactrim, which cover a lot. We’re keeping your other GVHD meds too—like prednisone and your eye drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do to avoid passing out again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep up your fluid intake, especially if you’re not eating much. Try not to skip meals. And if you feel lightheaded, sit down and elevate your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I check my blood pressure at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not necessary unless you feel unwell. But do follow up with your primary doctor and your transplant team. And we’ve rescheduled your cognitive neurology appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no dizziness, stable vitals. We’re ready to send you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—I stop fluconazole and keep everything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And call your oncologist about it. Stay hydrated, and if you feel faint again, sit down and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better and more aware of what to watch for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after experiencing syncope in the waiting room of a clinic, preceded by lightheadedness and no food or fluid intake that morning. Initial evaluation revealed hypotension, metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate, with no evidence of cardiac ischemia on serial troponins or EKG changes. A CT chest ruled out pulmonary embolism but incidentally showed new mild C7 and T2 vertebral compression fractures, deemed chronic and asymptomatic. She was treated with IV fluids, leading to stabilization of vital signs and resolution of symptoms. Fluconazole was discontinued due to QT prolongation risk. She remained stable on telemetry, with no arrhythmias, and was discharged home with instructions to increase oral hydration and follow up with her oncologist and primary care providers.
